summary: Defines BinaryTime, a new ASN.1 type that represents date and time as a number. It also defines a binary-signing-time attribute for CMS SignedData and AuthenticatedData as an alternative to the signing-time attribute from RFC 5652.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines a way to write a date and time as a single whole number instead of a string of digits and letters. It also defines a signing-time attribute that uses that number, so a signed message can carry its claim about time in a smaller form. The number is not proof of when the signing happened; the recipient decides whether to trust it.

subtitle: A date and time written as one whole number of seconds, plus a signing-time attribute that uses it.

tldr.problem: The ASN.1 time types UTCTime and GeneralizedTime are text values that are bulky and awkward to compare when the two values are given in different time zones, while many operating systems already keep time as a plain integer.
tldr.mechanism: BinaryTime is an ASN.1 INTEGER counting seconds, excluding leap seconds, since midnight UTC on 1 January 1970. The binary-signing-time attribute carries a BinaryTime value in CMS SignedData and AuthenticatedData.
tldr.outcome: The values are smaller and easier to compare than the older types, but the attribute still proves nothing about when signing really happened. The recipient decides whether to trust it.

today: RFC 6019 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It replaced RFC 4049, an earlier document with the same title that specified the same ASN.1 type.

sections.title: Why Another Time Format
sections.content:
This document specifies a new ASN.1 type for representing time: BinaryTime. It can be used for date and time values.

The document also specifies an alternative to the signing-time attribute used with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) SignedData and AuthenticatedData content types, so that the BinaryTime type can be used instead of the traditional UTCTime and GeneralizedTime types.
sections.plainLanguage: This document defines a new format for dates and times, and a way to use it inside signed messages. The format is a plain number of seconds, so programs that already keep time as a number can use it directly.

sections.title: The Advantages of an Integer
sections.content:
Many operating systems represent date and time as an integer, so this document defines an ASN.1 type that does the same. Some conversion may still be needed because of a different epoch or a different granularity, but an integer representation has several advantages over the UTCTime and GeneralizedTime types.

First, a BinaryTime value is smaller than either a UTCTime or a GeneralizedTime value. Second, in some operating systems the value can be used with little or no conversion. Where conversion is needed it requires only straightforward computation: if the byte order differs from the ASN.1 representation of an INTEGER, some byte manipulation is needed; if the epoch differs, addition or subtraction compensates; if the granularity is something other than seconds, multiplication or division compensates; and padding may be needed to convert the variable-length ASN.1 encoding of INTEGER into a fixed-length value.

Third, date comparison is very easy with BinaryTime. Comparing integers is easy even when multi-precision integers are involved, while comparing UTCTime or GeneralizedTime values given in different time zones can be complex. The document calls this a rare instance in which both memory and processor cycles can be saved.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers often keep time as one counting number. Writing time that way means less to store, less work to convert, and an easy way to tell which of two times came first even when they were written in different time zones.

sections.title: The BinaryTime Type
sections.content:
The BinaryTime ASN.1 type represents an absolute time and date. A positive integer value is used, based on coordinated universal time (UTC), which is also called Greenwich Mean Time and ZULU clock time. Its syntax is a single line: BinaryTime ::= INTEGER (0..MAX).

The integer is the number of seconds, excluding leap seconds, after midnight UTC on 1 January 1970. This representation of time is sometimes called UNIX time. The format cannot represent time values prior to that date.

The upper end is not fixed. The latest UTC time value that can be represented by a four-octet integer value is 03:14:07 on 19 January 2038, which is represented by the hexadecimal value 7FFFFFFF. Time values beyond that point are represented by integer values longer than four octets, and a five-octet integer value is sufficient to represent dates covering the next seventeen millennia.

The specification uses the variable-length encoding of INTEGER, which permits any time value after midnight UTC on 1 January 1970 to be represented. When an integer value consists of more than one octet, which includes almost all the time values of interest, the bits of the first octet and bit 8 of the second octet must not all be ones or all zeros. That rule ensures an integer value is always encoded in the smallest possible number of octets, but it means implementations cannot assume a fixed length for the value.
sections.plainLanguage: The clock starts counting seconds on 1 January 1970. The count leaves out leap seconds, and it cannot show any time before that date. If a counter runs out of room, the number just gets more digits, so the clock never has to stop.

sections.title: The binary-signing-time Attribute
sections.content:
The binary-signing-time attribute type specifies the time at which the signer (purportedly) performed the signing process. It is intended for the CMS SignedData content type, but it can also be used with the AuthenticatedData content type.

Its placement is strict. The attribute must be a signed attribute or an authenticated attribute. It must not be an unsigned attribute, an unauthenticated attribute, or an unprotected attribute. It is identified by id-aa-binarySigningTime, which is arc 46 under smime(16) aa(2), and its values have the ASN.1 type BinarySigningTime ::= BinaryTime.

In CMS the SignedAttributes syntax and the AuthAttributes syntax are each defined as a SET OF Attributes, yet the binary-signing-time attribute must have a single attribute value. There must not be zero or multiple instances of AttributeValue present. The SignedAttributes contained in the signerInfo structure within SignedData must not include multiple instances of the attribute, and the same holds for the AuthAttributes in an AuthenticatedData.
sections.plainLanguage: A signer can stamp a note saying when they signed, written as one number. There must be exactly one such stamp in a message, and it must be covered by the signature so nobody can swap it later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Use of the binary-signing-time attribute does not necessarily provide confidence in the time when the signature value was produced, so acceptance of a purported signing time is a matter of the recipient's discretion. RFC 3161 specifies a protocol for obtaining time stamps from a trusted entity, for a recipient who needs that confidence.

The original signing-time attribute defined in RFC 5652 has the same semantics as the attribute defined here, so only one of the two should be present in the signedAttrs of a SignerInfo object or in the authAttrs of an AuthenticatedData object. If both of them are present, they must provide the same date and time.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can write any time on a note they sign, so the note alone is not proof. If you need proof, ask a trusted clock-keeper to stamp it. If a message carries two time notes, they must agree.

sections.title: The ASN.1 Module
sections.content: Appendix A gives the ASN.1 module needed to implement the specification, meant to be used in conjunction with the ASN.1 modules in CMS. It uses IMPLICIT TAGS and contains three definitions: the BinaryTime type, the object identifier id-aa-binarySigningTime, and BinarySigningTime.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix is the formal recipe card that computers read, repeating the same three definitions given in the text.

items.title: Epoch
items.text: Seconds since midnight UTC on 1 January 1970.

items.title: Length
items.text: Variable, so a reader cannot assume a fixed size.

viz.caption: THE DEFINITIONS IN THE APPENDIX A ASN.1 MODULE

data.title: BinarySigningTimeModule
data.code:
BinaryTime ::= INTEGER (0..MAX)

id-aa-binarySigningTime OBJECT IDENTIFIER ::= { iso(1)
    member-body(2) us(840) rsadsi(113549) pkcs(1) pkcs9(9)
    smime(16) aa(2) 46 }

BinarySigningTime ::= BinaryTime
